en: The term *vṛddhi* refers to the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*.
The vowels a, e, and o are termed guṇa.
The *iK* vowels [are designated as] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
There is no elision of a root-vowel (*dhātu*) before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
And [the substitution of guṇa and vṛddhi] does not take place before suffixes marked with the markers K and Ṅ.
The roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, as well as [a root] having the augment *iṭ*, [are termed dhātu].
Conjunctions are those [atoms] that are immediately adjacent. // PS 1.1.7 //
A sound articulated through both the mouth and the nose is called *anunāsika* (nasalized).
That which has the same place of articulation and effort is homogeneous (savarṇa).
Neither a vowel nor a consonant [is called a *saṃyoga*]. (PS 1.1.10)
A dual ending containing the vowels ī, ū, or e is called *pragṛhya*.
The word *adas* is called *māt*.
A particle (nipāta) consisting of a single vowel, excluding the vowels *a* and *ā*, [is called pragṛhya].
Thus it is said. (PS 1.1.15)

In the case of a perfective suffix (sambuddhi), the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of *śākalya* occurs when the particle *iti* follows, provided it is not part of a Vedic seer's utterance (*anārṣa*).
The *u* and *ū* [substitutes] are applied in place of the final vowel of a verbal root.
And the vowels *ī* and *ū* [are called *pragṛhya*] when they stand in the sense of the locative case.
The roots *dā* and *dhā*, with the exception of *adāp*, are designated as *ghu*.
As with the beginning and the end, so it is with the one.
The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*.
The suffixes bahu, gaṇa, vatu, and ḍati are numerals.
Those ending in -ṣ and -n are called ṣaṭ.
And [the suffix] ḍati [is also applied]. (PS 1.1.25)
The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are termed *niṣṭhā*.
The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*).
In a Bahuvrīhi compound, there is optionally the substitution of *dik* for *diś* before a word ending in *samāsanta*.
Not [is there elision] in a bahuvrīhi compound. (PS 1.1.29)
In a compound with a third case [as the prior member]. (PS 1.1.30)
And [the first member retains its original accent] in a copulative compound (dvandva).
The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies before the suffix *jas*.
And [the suffixes] -prathama, -carama, -taya, -alpa, -ardha, -katipaya, and -nema [are also used as indeclinables].

The terms *pūrva* (east/front), *para* (other/far), *avara* (near/this side), *dakṣiṇa* (south/right), *uttara* (north/left), *apara* (west/back), and *adhara* (below) [are used] when there is a spatial relation (*vyavasthā*), provided they do not function as proper names (*asañjñā*).
The word *sva* [is used] in the sense of "one's own wealth" when it does not refer to a kinsman.
The intermediate space is [the location] between the upper garment and the lower garment.
The particles beginning with *svar* and those that are indeclinables (*nipāta*) are called *avyaya*.
And a taddhita derivative that does not take all case endings [is also called avyaya].
A *kṛt* suffix ending in *ej* is called a verbal root (*dhātu*).
The suffixes *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun* [are called *kṛt*]. // PS_1.1.40 //
And the *avyayībhāva* [compound] is also [neuter].
The neuter case endings [N] and [Su] are termed *sarvanāmasthāna*.
The suffix *suṭ* is applied [after a verbal root] when it is not a neuter [noun].
The term "vibhāṣā" means "optionally," expressed as "either... or not."
The semivowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ* undergo *samprasāraṇa*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the group beginning with *gāṅkuṭa*, provided it is not preceded by a *ṇi* or *ṅi*.
The seed is desired. (PS 1.2.2)
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies after the word *ūrṇa*.
A sārvadhātuka suffix that is not marked with P is [also called ārdhadhātuka].
The *liṭ* [affix] is *kit* when not preceded by a conjunct consonant. *Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.5*.
And [the suffix *kta* is applied] after the roots *indh* and *bhū*.
The suffix *ktvā* is applied after the roots *mṛḍ*, *amṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas*.
And after the roots rud, vid, muṣ, grah, svap, and pracch, the suffix saṃ is also [used].
An *ik* vowel followed by a *jhal* consonant [is elided].
And [the final consonant] after a word ending in a hal (consonant) [is also elided].
The suffixes *liṅ* and *sic* [are used] in the *ātmanepada*.
And [the augment *u* is applied] after [a verbal root ending in] *ū*. PS_1,2.12.
Or [it is] a verbal root (gam). PS_1.2.13.
The suffix *sic* is applied after the root *han*.
Yama [is the deity] in the sense of smelling.
The Vibhāṣā [states] that there is [a fault] in marrying [a girl]. (PS 1.2.16)
The augment *iṭ* is applied after the roots *sthā* and *ghu*.
The suffix *ktvā* does not take the augment *iṭ*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs after the roots *śīṅ*, *svidi*, *midi*, *kṣvidi*, and *dhṛṣ*.
The word *mṛṣa* is used in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*). (PS 1.2.20)
After a root having *u* as its penultimate letter, the suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied when the formation denotes either an abstract state (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*).
The suffix *ktvā* is also applied after the root *pūṅ*.
A suffix beginning with *t* or *th* is optionally added after a word ending in *tha* or *pha*, provided it is not part of a verbal root (*upadhāt*).
And [the suffixes] -vañci, -luñci, and ṛta [are applied after the root √chid].
The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *tṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, and *kṛś* when followed by the patronymic *kāśyapa*.
A light vowel (rala) followed by *v* or *y*, and preceded by a consonant (*upadhā*), undergoes *guṇa* substitution; likewise, the suffix *saṃ* [undergoes the same].
A vowel (ac) having the duration of an u-sound is termed short (hrasva), long (dīrgha), or protracted (pluta).
And from this [it follows]. (PS 1.2.28)
A vowel pronounced with high pitch is called udātta (acute).
The low-pitched accent is the *anudātta*.
A combination [of udātta and anudātta] is called svarita.
Of that [syllable], the first half-mora is acute.
The single accent (eka-śruti) is used for addressing someone from a distance.
In sacrificial rites, [the rules regarding *pluti* do not apply] to the *ajapa*, *nyūṅkha*, and *sāman* chants. (PS 1.2.34)
Or the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance may be at a higher pitch.
In the Vedic language, there is optionality.
In the Subrahmaṇyā formula, however, a circumflex vowel becomes acute.
The [vowel] following the words *deva* and *brahman* is unaccented (anudātta).
In the *saṃhitā*, [the *kampa* accent] occurs for the *anudātta* syllables following a *svarita*.
A vowel following an acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita) accent is pronounced more depressed (sannatara).
A single-letter suffix that is not joined [with another element] is called *apṛkta*.
A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have the same grammatical referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is called a *karmadhāraya*.
In a compound, that which is designated by the nominative case is the *upasarjana*.
And [a word] in the same case-ending [is compounded], provided it does not occur as the first member. (PS 1.2.44)
That which possesses meaning, being neither a verbal root nor an affix, is a nominal stem (prātipadika).
And [the categories of] *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, and compounds [are also included]. (Pāṇini 1.2.46)
The final vowel of a nominal stem becomes short when it is in the neuter gender.
The feminine suffix is elided when it is an *upasarjana*.
There is elision [of the feminine suffix] when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix.
The [substitution of] "id" occurs for the word "goṇī" [in the sense of "cow"].
When a suffix denoting diminution (*lup*) is applied, the gender and number are like those of the original base.
And [there is no compounding] of qualifiers with that which has not yet been born (ajāti). PS 1.2.52.
That [inference] is not to be taught, because its validity depends on conventional designation (saṃjñā).
Or because of the non-manifestation of yoga. (PS 1.2.54)
And when that [object] is absent, there would be non-perception, according to the criterion of yoga.
The statement that the primary condition (pradhāna-pratyaya) has a specific meaning [is not tenable], because the object is established by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And this is the same when time is a subordinate element.
When a genus is denoted, the plural may optionally be used for a single individual.
And [the suffixes] du and śas are substituted for the word "asmad" when it denotes duality.
And [the same applies] when the moon is in the lunar mansions of Phalgunī or Proṣṭhapadā.
In the Vedic language, however, the dual form *punarvasū* takes the singular ending.
And [the same applies] to the two Viśākhās. PS_1.2.62.
In the case of the dual compound of the two constellations Tiṣya and Punarvasu, the dual number is always used instead of the plural.
When words ending in the same case-ending follow one another, only one remains, provided they are accompanied by the word *sūpa*.
An old man [is compared] with a young man, provided that the distinction between them consists solely in those characteristics.
And the feminine [stem] is treated like the masculine.
A man [is the agent] with a woman. // PS 1.2.67 //
The words *bhrātṛ* (brother) and *putra* (son) [form a compound] with *svasṛ* (sister) and *duhitṛ* (daughter), respectively.
A neuter [noun] followed by a non-neuter [noun] forms a single compound, and its gender may optionally be that of the latter member.
The father [is the same] as the mother.
The father-in-law [is expressed by the suffix *aṇ*], and so is the mother-in-law.
The pronouns beginning with *tyad* are always [used] with all [other pronouns].
A woman among herds of domestic animals that are not yet young. (PS 1.2.73)
The verbal roots begin with *bhū* and so forth.
In the Upadeśa, a vowel followed by an anusvāra is called *it*.
The final [element] among those [elements] beginning with the *hal* (consonants) [is called an *it*].
In a case-ending (vibhakti), the [final] *t*, *u*, and *m* are not elided.
The suffixes beginning with ñ, ṇ, and ṭu, as well as those marked with u, are kṛt suffixes.
The letter ṣ is [the augment] of the suffix. (PS 1.3.6)
The *laś* [suffixes] are called *kvat* when they are not *taddhita*.
There is its elision. (PS 1.3.9)
The subsequent mention of an equal number of items follows their respective order.
The governing authority is indicated by the svarita accent. (Pāṇini 1.3.11)
The Ātmanepada [suffixes] are used for roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (anudātta) or the letter ṅ.
[The genitive case is used] for the agent and the object [of the action]. (PS 1.3.13)
The [kṛt] affix *kha* is used in the sense of the agent when there is a reciprocal action.
Not after [roots] meaning motion or injury. (PS 1.3.15)
And [the suffix *kṛt* is applied] after the upapadas *itaretara* and *anyonya*. (PS 1.3.16)
Nor [should one enter] among the people. // PS_1,3.17 //
The root √kṛ follows [the same rules] after the prefixes pari, vi, and ava.
The prefix *vi* and *parā* are used before the root *ji*.
The substitution of *d* for the final *aṅ* occurs when it does not mean "moving the nose."
The root *krīḍ* (to play) is also [governed by the same rule] when preceded by the prefixes *anu*, *saṃ*, and *pari*.
The root *sthā* takes the prefix *ātmanepada* when preceded by *sam*, *ava*, *pra*, or *vi*.
And [the same applies] to the faults known as *prakāśana* (manifestation) and *stheya* (obstinacy). PS 1.3.23.
The prefix *ud-* is used in the sense of "not upward" (*anūrdhva*) action.
The *upā* [prefix] is used when the root *man* functions as a verbal suffix (*karaṇa*).
And [the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used] after a verb that does not take an object (*akarmaka*).
The root *tap* [takes the ātmanepada endings] when preceded by the prefixes *ud* and *vi*.
[The substitution of *ātmanepada* endings occurs] after the root *yama-* and *hana-*, when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
The roots √gam, √ṛcch, √prach, √svar, √ṛ, √śru, and √vidi (vid) are treated like √sā when followed by the suffix -am.
The root *hve* (to call) takes the prefix *ātmanepada* when preceded by *ni*, *sam*, *upa*, or *vi*.
The prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of competition (*spardhā*).
The verb *kṛ* (to do/make) is used with the locative case when it signifies: smelling, throwing down, serving, daring, striving, speaking, and employing. (Pāṇini 1.3.32)
The preposition *adhi* [is used] in the sense of overcoming (*prasahana*).
The root *vi* [is used in the sense of motion] when its object is sound.
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after a verbal root that does not require an object (*akarmaka*).
The root *ni* is used in the sense of honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowledge, wages, counting, and expenditure. (Pāṇini 1.3.36)
And [the ātman is the agent] when the action resides in the body which is the locus of the agent. (PS 1.3.37)
The sequence [of the suffixes] occurs in the senses of function (vṛtti), creation (sarga), and protection (tāyana).
[The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *i* when preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *parā*. PS 1.3.39.
The prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of rising up. (Pāṇini 1.3.40)
The root *vi* is used in the sense of moving the feet.
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after the prefixes *pra* and *upa*, when they are semantically connected [with the following verbal root]. (PS 1.3.42)
Or [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root that does not have a prefix (*anupasarga*).
The suffix *jñā* is used after a verb when there is a denial of knowledge.
And also after a root that does not have an object.
The suffix *man* is used after the roots *sam* and *prati*, except when expressing the sense of "thinking about" (*anādhyāne*).
The verb *vad* is used in the sense of speaking, addressing, knowing, exerting effort, disagreeing, and inviting. (Pāṇini 1.3.47)
[The suffix *kvin* is applied] after [a verbal root] denoting articulate speech, when there is an act of uttering [that speech].
The suffix *an* is applied after a root that does not express an action, provided it is intransitive.
Vibhāṣā is [the term for] idle chatter. (PS 1.3.50)
The suffix *grah* is applied after the verbal root *av*.
It is equal in its commitment. (PS 1.3.52)
The root *ud* [meaning "to move upwards"] is [used] with an object when it is transitive.
The particle *saṃ* [is used] when joined with a word in the third case.
And [the word] *dāṇ* [is used] for that which has the sense of the fourth case. *PS_1.3.55*
The suffix *yamaṅ* is applied after the root *upā-dā* when it means "to take for oneself."
The suffix *san* is applied after the roots *jñā*, *śru*, *smṛ*, and *dṛś*.
The knower is not atomic. (PS 1.3.58)
The suffix *ātmanepada* is used after the root *śru* when preceded by the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ*.
The substitution of *ś* for the root *śad* occurs when followed by an affix marked with *ś*.
The substitution of *a* for the root *mṛ* occurs before the suffixes of the *luṅ* (aorist) and *liṅ* (precative).
As before, the suffix *san* [is applied]. (PS 1.3.62)
The verb *kṛ* is employed after the verbal root [ending in the suffix *ām*], just as it is when the suffix *ām* follows [the same root]. (Pāṇini 1.3.63)
The root *yuj* (to join) following the prefixes *pra-* and *upa-* [forms the Ātmanepada], except when used with sacrificial vessels.
The root *kṣṇu* is treated as *sama*.
The root *bhuja* is used in the sense of protecting.
When there is a *ṇic* suffix, that which was the object [of the root] becomes the agent [of the causative], provided it is not a state of mind (*anādhyāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.52)
The suffix *smyu* is used after the root *bhī* when fear is the cause.
The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* are used in the sense of deceiving.
The root *li* is used in the senses of honoring and making someone humble.
The affix *ghañ* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *mithyā*, provided that the action is repeated.
The *ātmanepada* affixes are used after a verbal root marked with a svarita accent or the marker *ñ*, when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.
The word *apāt* is a substitute for *vadaḥ*.
And [the suffix] *ṇic* [is applied after a verbal root]. (Pāṇini 1.3.74)
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *yam-* when preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *ud*, or *āṅ*, except in the sense of "tying a knot."
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *jñā* when it is not preceded by a prefix.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, [the suffix] is used when the meaning is understood through a co-occurring word (*upapada*).
From the remaining [roots], the *parasmaipada* endings are used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
The root *kṛ* [is used in the ātmanepada after the prefixes] *anu* and *parā*.
The suffix *kṣip* is applied after the prefixes *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*.
The eastward-flowing [wind]. // PS_1,3.81 //
The suffix *mṛṣ* is used in the sense of "excluding."
The root *ram* [takes the ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes *vi*, *āṅ*, and *pari*.
And [the augment *iṭ* is applied] after an *upadhā*. (PS 1.3.84)
According to the Vibhāṣā, [the suffix *sa* is applied] after an intransitive verb (*akarmaka*).

The suffix *niṣṭhā* (the *kta* and *ktavatu* participles) does not take the augment *iṭ* after the roots *budha*, *yudha*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, and *srub* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*.
And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after verbal roots meaning "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*) and "moving" (*calana*).
In the case of an atom, [motion arises] from an actionless agent that possesses consciousness.
The suffix *kyap* is not applied after the verbal roots √dam, √yam, √añc, √as, √parimuha, √ruc, √nṛt, √vad, or √vas.
Or [the suffixes of the parasmaipada and ātmanepada] are used after a verb ending in *kyaṣ*.
The *luṅ* suffixes are applied after the root *dhyai*.
After the roots *vṛt* and those that follow it, the suffixes *syat* (the future marker) and *san* (the desiderative marker) are optionally treated as having the *ārdhadhātuka* designation.
And [the affix *luṅ*] is also applied after the root *klup* in the sense of the past tense (*luṅ*).
Up to and including the word *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation for a single grammatical element.
When there is a conflict between rules, the subsequent one takes effect.
Feminine stems ending in /ī/ and /ū/ are called *nadī*.
Those [stems] that do not have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes are not feminine.
I go.
And [the final vowel of a nominal stem] is short before an affix marked with Ṅ or Ṭ.
The remaining [consonants], with the exception of *gh*, *y*, *s*, and *kha*, [are called *jhal*].
The word *pati* [is compounded] only in a compound (*samāsa*). (Pāṇini 1.4.8)
In the Vedic language, [the genitive] joined with a word ending in the sixth case-ending is optionally [retained].
A short [vowel] is light.
In a conjunct consonant, [the first member] is heavy. (PS 1.4.11)
And [the vowel] *dīrgha* (long). PS_1,4.12 //
Since it is a rule concerning suffixes, that which begins with the element before the suffix is the *aṅga* (base) when a suffix follows.
That which ends in a nominal suffix (sup) or a verbal suffix (tiṅ) is a word (pada).
The particle *kye* is not [a cause for the elision of the initial vowel] of the word *naḥ*.
And [the suffix] *siti*. // PS_1,4.16 //
The term *svādi* [is used] except when it occurs in a case-ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*).
He begged for alms.
The suffixes *ta* and *sa* [are applied] in the sense of the matup-affix (*matvartha*).
In the Vedic language, [the suffixes] -maya and so forth [are applied after a word ending in the sixth case]. PS_1.4.20.
The plural number is used for many things. (PS 1.4.21)
The dual and singular endings are used for two and one, respectively.
In the context of a kāraka. // PS_1,4.23 //
That which remains fixed when there is a departure is the *apādāna*.
For verbs meaning "to fear" or "to protect," the cause of fear [is the object]. (PS 1.4.25)
The root *parā-aj* [is used] in the sense of "not being able to endure. (Pāṇini 1.4.26)
In the case of verbs meaning "to ward off," that which is desired [is the object].
In the case of disappearance, it is that by which one desires to become invisible. (PS 1.4.28)
The verb *ākhyā* (to tell) [is used in the fourth case] when it denotes the act of instructing.
The source of the agent of birth is the *prakṛti*.
The origin of the intermediate space (bhuvas). PS_1.4.31.
That person whom one intends to reach by means of an action is the recipient (sampradāna).
In the case of verbs meaning "to find pleasure," the person who is pleased is the recipient (saṃpradāna).
In the case of the roots √ślāgh (to praise), √hnu (to deny), √sthā (to stand), and √śap (to curse), the person being informed [of the action] is the object.
In the case of the root *dhṛ* (to owe), the creditor is the agent.
In the case of the verb *spṛh* ("to desire"), that which is desired is [the sampradāna kāraka].
In the case of roots meaning anger (*krudh*), malice (*druh*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and censure (*asūyā*), the dative case is used for the person toward whom the anger is directed. (Pāṇini 1.4.37)
When the prefixes *upa* and *ni* are used with the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to injure), that which is acted upon is called the object (*karman*).
When the verbs √rādh and √īkṣ take the genitive case, it signifies an inquiry about that person.
When the roots *śru* preceded by the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ* are used, the agent of the preceding action [is called the *sampradāna*].
And [the rule applies] to *anu* and *prati* when they are followed by *gṛṇa*.
The most effective means is the instrument (karaṇa). PS 1.4.42.
And [the word] *divaḥ* [governs the genitive case when used with] the word *karman*. (PS 1.4.43)
In the case of purchasing, the recipient is optionally designated as the *sampradāna* (indirect object).
The substratum is the locus.
The object of the roots √śī (to lie down), √sthā (to stand), and √ās (to sit) [is called adhikaraṇa].
And one is attached. // PS_1,4.47 //
The roots √vas preceded by the prefixes upa, anu, adhi, and ā take the locative case.
The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*.
And likewise, that which is connected [to the action] but is not intended [by the agent]. (PS 1.4.50)
And that which is not otherwise specified [is also called the object]. (Pāṇini 1.4.51)

In the case of roots meaning protection (*guti*), cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or having sound as their object (*śabda-karman*), as well as intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), that which is the agent (*kartā*) in the *aṇ* [causative] is [the object] in the *ṇic* [causative]. (Pāṇini 1.4.52)
The accusative case may optionally be used after the roots *hṛ* (to carry) and *kṛ* (to do/make).
The agent is one who is independent. (PS 1.4.54)
And the instigator of that [action] is also a cause (hetu). (PS 1.4.55)
The particles [beginning with] *ca* and ending with *eva* are called *nipāta* (particles), provided they occur before the word *īśvara*.
The particles beginning with *ca* are used when not denoting a substance (*asattve*).
The words beginning with *pra* [are prepositions when they are compounded with a verbal root]. PS 1.4.58.
The *upasargas* [are designated as such] when they are joined with a verbal root (*kriyā*).
And [the word *gati*] also [denotes the action of going]. (PS 1.4.60)
And the words beginning with *ūry-* [are treated as indeclinables], as well as those derived from the suffix * cvi* and the word *ḍāc*.
And an imitation [of a sound] is also [treated as a *kṣaipra*], provided it does not end in the vowel *i*.
